prompt: A team buys an observability product and points it at production. What will its dashboards show about a value the code never records?
hint: A dashboard draws what it was sent.

choices.text: Nothing: no tool shows a number that was never produced
choices.why: Right. Somebody has to decide what the system says about itself before any tool can draw it.

choices.text: An estimate, inferred from the values it does receive
choices.why: A product can compute from what it receives, and a value never sent is not among them.

choices.text: The value, read directly from the process's memory
choices.why: No tool reads arbitrary variables from a running service; something has to emit them.

choices.text: A gap, which the vendor fills in once the agent learns the code
choices.why: An agent can instrument libraries it knows, but it cannot guess a business value nobody recorded.

prompt: Which question is observability rather than monitoring?
hint: One of them nobody planned for.

choices.text: Is the error rate above two per cent?
choices.why: A threshold somebody already knew to watch: monitoring.

choices.text: Is the disk of the database server more than 90% full?
choices.why: A known condition, checked continuously: monitoring.

choices.text: Why are checkouts with one card brand slower since Tuesday?
choices.why: Right. Nobody wrote a check for it in advance; it is asked after the fact, of signals rich enough to answer.

choices.text: Is the storefront answering its health check?
choices.why: Up or down is the classic monitoring question.

prompt: Match each signal to what one of it is.

pairs.right: A number sampled over time, with a few labels
One event, written when it happened, with fields
One request's path through every service it touched

right_distractors: A copy of the database taken every night

prompt: In the lab, which part was written for the course rather than installed?

choices.text: Prometheus and Alertmanager
choices.why: Both run from their official images, unmodified.

choices.text: The shop: every container whose image is `shop:1.4.0`
choices.why: Right. The shop is the thing being observed; everything that watches it is real software.

choices.text: The OpenTelemetry Collector, rewritten to keep the lab small
choices.why: It is the contrib distribution, unmodified.

choices.text: Grafana's dashboards and its data sources
choices.why: Grafana is the official image; lesson 7 builds the dashboards.

prompt: Put the shop's services in the order a paid checkout reaches them.
hint: The customer, the order, the money, the e-mail.

prompt: Which shapes of a production system does the lab's shop have? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: HTTP calls between services
choices.why: Yes: storefront to orders to payments.

choices.text: A database
choices.why: Yes, PostgreSQL behind orders.

choices.text: A queue
choices.why: Yes, RabbitMQ between orders and mailer.

choices.text: A scheduled job
choices.why: Yes, the nightly report.

choices.text: A content delivery network in front of the storefront
choices.why: There is none; the storefront is published on 127.0.0.1.

prompt: You open `localhost:9090` from another computer on the same network as the lab and nothing answers. Why?

choices.text: Prometheus listens only while a lesson is running
choices.why: It runs as long as the lab is up.

choices.text: Every port is published on 127.0.0.1, so only the lab machine itself reaches it
choices.why: Right, and `localhost` on the other computer is that computer anyway.

choices.text: Port 9090 belongs to Grafana, which needs a password
choices.why: Grafana is on 3000; 9090 is Prometheus.

choices.text: Docker refuses connections until the lab is started again from nothing
choices.why: Starting again empties the volumes; it has nothing to do with who may connect.

prompt: With payments slowed down, the checkout answered `201 in 1.536103 s`. What would a check that only asks "did it answer with a success code?" report?

choices.text: That everything is fine
choices.why: Right. The order was stored and charged; only the time is wrong, and this check does not look at time.

choices.text: That the checkout failed, because of the time
choices.why: The check never reads the time.

choices.text: That payments is slow
choices.why: From outside, the services behind the storefront are invisible.

choices.text: Nothing until the second request arrives
choices.why: It judges each request on its own.

prompt: Healthy, the checkout took 0.036398 s. To the nearest whole millisecond, how many milliseconds is that?
Why can no amount of studying the slow `201` tell you which service spent the time?

choices.text: Because `curl` rounds the time to the millisecond
choices.why: It prints microseconds; the problem is not precision.

choices.text: Because the storefront hides the services it calls for security
choices.why: Nothing is hidden on purpose; the answer just has no field for it.

choices.text: The answer carries one status and one total, and the split between services was never put in it
choices.why: Right. Four services, a database and a queue collapse into one number at the edge.

choices.text: Because the slow part was the network between `curl` and the storefront
choices.why: The trace shows it was payments; the network here is one machine.

prompt: The histogram's `_sum` was 167.50 seconds over a `_count` of 111 checkouts. What was the mean checkout time, in seconds, to two decimal places?
The bucket `le="1.0"` reads 2 and `le="2.5"` reads 111. How many checkouts took more than one second and at most two and a half?

choices.text: 111, because that is the value of the 2.5 bucket
choices.why: Each bucket counts everything at or below its bound, including the 2 fast ones.
Right: 111 at or under 2.5, minus 2 at or under 1.
Those are the ones at or under one second.

choices.text: It cannot be known from buckets
choices.why: The difference between two adjacent buckets is exactly that count.

prompt: Prometheus reported a 99th percentile of 2.485 s, while every slow checkout waited the same 1.5 s in payments. What produced the difference?
hint: What does a histogram know about one request?

choices.text: A few requests were lost between the scrape and the query
choices.why: Losing requests would lower the counts, not raise the estimate above every real value.

choices.text: The 99th percentile includes the time Prometheus took to scrape
choices.why: Scraping does not add to the measured durations.

choices.text: The histogram only knows the bucket, so Prometheus assumed the 109 requests between 1 and 2.5 s were spread evenly
choices.why: Right. The estimate is read off that assumption, and the real values were all near the bottom of the bucket.

choices.text: `rate()` multiplies the result by the length of its window, so a window of two minutes doubles every percentile the query returns
choices.why: `rate()` is a per-second average over the window; nothing is doubled.

prompt: Why does the checkout histogram cost the same at a thousand checkouts as at a million?
hint: What grows: the lines or the numbers on them?

choices.text: Only its numbers grow
choices.why: Right. A metric aggregates; traffic changes values, not the number of series.

choices.text: Prometheus throws away every request after the first thousand
choices.why: Nothing is discarded; every request is counted.

choices.text: It is compressed more as it grows
choices.why: Compression is not why; the count of lines is fixed.

choices.text: It is only read once a day
choices.why: It is scraped every fifteen seconds.

prompt: In the line `..._bucket{le="0.5",...} 2.0`, the label `le` stands for less than or ___.
What can the storefront's log line say that the checkout histogram cannot?

choices.text: How many checkouts there were in the last two minutes
choices.why: Counting over time is the metric's job, and it does it cheaply.

choices.text: Which order it was, which product, and how it ended
choices.why: Right: order 111, a kettle, paid. A log line is one event with its own values.

choices.text: Where the second and a half was spent
choices.why: No line mentions the wait; nobody wrote one.

choices.text: The 99th percentile of checkout time
choices.why: A percentile is computed over many requests, from a metric.

prompt: Why could `grep` on the trace id find the same checkout in the logs of `payments` and `orders`?

choices.text: Because the services share one log file
choices.why: Each container writes its own output.

choices.text: Because the trace id is the order number written in hexadecimal, so it is the same wherever the order goes
choices.why: It is a random 128-bit id, unrelated to the order.

choices.text: Each service logs the id of the request it serves, and the id travelled with it
choices.why: Right. Lesson 4 is how it travels.

choices.text: Because Loki copies the field into every service's lines
choices.why: Loki stores lines; it does not add fields to them.

prompt: The lab runs on one machine, so `docker compose logs` found every line. Why does it also send them to Loki?

choices.text: Production runs on many machines, and one place that holds every line is what lets the same search reach all of them
choices.why: Right. Lesson 9 is centralised logs.

choices.text: `docker compose logs` drops lines older than one minute
choices.why: It keeps them; the problem is reach, not age.

choices.text: Loki is faster at grep than grep
choices.why: Speed on one machine is not the reason.

choices.text: The JSON is only valid once Loki parses it
choices.why: The lines are JSON as written.

prompt: Reading the logs of the slow checkout, where do you find the 1.5 second wait?
hint: Who would have had to write it?

choices.text: In the `level` field of the payments line
choices.why: It says INFO; the level is not a duration.

choices.text: In the orders line, as `status`
choices.why: That field is not there, and status is the outcome.

choices.text: Nowhere; nobody logged it
choices.why: Right. A log says only what a program chose to say.

choices.text: In the storefront line, as `outcome`
choices.why: `outcome` is `paid`.

prompt: In the trace, `payments` spent almost all its time in a child span. What does that child span tell you that `POST /charge` alone did not?

choices.text: Which step inside payments took the time
choices.why: Right: waiting for the card network, named by the code that waited.

choices.text: That the charge failed
choices.why: It was approved; the trace carries no error.

choices.text: That orders called payments twice
choices.why: There is one call.

choices.text: How many checkouts were slow
choices.why: A trace is one request; counting is the metric's job.

prompt: Which spans in the slow checkout's trace come from a service that has no OpenTelemetry code of its own? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `INSERT`
choices.why: Yes, from orders' database driver, instrumented automatically.

choices.text: `UPDATE`
choices.why: Yes, the same.

choices.text: `POST /orders`
choices.why: Yes, from Flask, instrumented automatically.

choices.text: `wait for the card network`
choices.why: That one payments' own code opened by hand.

choices.text: `orders.placed process`
choices.why: mailer's own code opened it.

prompt: The storefront's span took about as long as everything under it. If the wait in payments were removed, which spans would get shorter?
hint: A parent lasts at least as long as the children it waits for.

choices.text: Only `wait for the card network`
choices.why: Every span waiting on it would also shrink.

choices.text: Only the mailer's spans, which run last
choices.why: The mailer works after the queue and is not waiting on payments.

choices.text: The wait and every span waiting on it, up to `POST /checkout`
choices.why: Right. That chain is the critical path, and lesson 11 reads it.

choices.text: None, because a span measures the code that runs and not the time spent waiting
choices.why: A span measures wall time from start to end, waits included.

prompt: Match each question to the signal that answers it first.

pairs.left: Are checkouts slower than usual right now?
Which service spent the time in this checkout?
What exactly did payments decide for order 111?

prompt: What lets you go from the slow trace to the log lines of the same request?
hint: It is a field both carry.

choices.text: The timestamp, matched to the second
choices.why: Many requests share a second; time narrows the search but does not join.

choices.text: Its id, which the shop writes into each line
choices.why: Right. It is the join between the two signals.

choices.text: The service name, which both signals carry
choices.why: Every request of that service shares it.

choices.text: The order id, which traces always record
choices.why: Only where the code put it there, and it does not exist for requests that are not orders.

prompt: An alert fires on the checkout percentile at 3 a.m. Which order of looking wastes the least time?
hint: From the many to the one.

choices.text: Logs first, reading every line written since midnight until something stands out
choices.why: Without a service or a request to look for, this is reading the haystack.

choices.text: Traces first, opening them at random
choices.why: Random traces are mostly the healthy majority.

choices.text: The metric for when, a slow trace from then for where, its logs for why
choices.why: Right. Each step narrows the next one.

choices.text: Restart every service and then read the metric
choices.why: Restarting first destroys the evidence and may not help.

prompt: Metrics say that something is wrong, traces say ___ it is wrong, and logs say why.
